title: Building a Column from Spiking Neurons
intro: A practical plan for building a cortical column from spiking neurons: a clear first target, the architecture, which neuron model and learning rule go where, why inhibition matters most, a minimum viable column with its numbers, the milestones in order, and what is known versus speculative. The pages under the Building an SNN Column step of the Computational Cortical Columns path go deeper on simulators, chips, encoders, evaluation, a staged roadmap and pitfalls.

blocks.text: Start from a clear target

'Make a cortical column' is too vague to finish. A useful first target, taken from the Thousand Brains Theory (#/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/thousand-brains), is: a column that, given a stream of (movement, sensed feature) pairs from touching objects, learns a set of objects without labels and recognises a learned object within a few touches, and that several such columns, voting, recognise it faster. Everything below serves that target. It is concrete, it can be measured (touches to recognition, accuracy, number of objects learned), and each stage works and can be tested on its own.
From reading to running

The rest of the Computational Cortical Columns path tells you what a cortical column might compute. This page, and the pages of the Building an SNN Column step (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/building-an-snn-column), are about getting one to run: which simulator or chip to use, how to turn data into spikes, how to tell whether the thing you built is working, in which order to build it, and which mistakes cost people weeks. Think of it as the lab manual that goes with the textbook.

The guiding idea is incremental validation. A cortical column model has many interacting parts — spiking neurons, excitation/inhibition balance, plasticity, homeostasis, sparse codes, dendritic segments, location signals and lateral voting. If you wire all of them together at once and the network is silent or epileptic, you will not know which part is to blame. If instead each stage is checked against a known reference (an analytic f–I curve, a published firing-rate regime, a replicated benchmark), every failure is local and cheap to find.
Why tools and order matter

items: Tool choice shapes the model you end up with. Equation-level simulators (Brian2, NEST) make biophysics easy and gradient training hard; PyTorch-based libraries (snnTorch, Norse) are the reverse; neuromorphic chips impose fan-in, weight precision and learning-rule constraints that you should design around from the start rather than discover at the end.

Encoders decide what your column can learn. An HTM-style column expects sparse distributed input with semantic overlap; a Diehl & Cook-style STDP layer expects Poisson rate input. Feeding the wrong kind of code into a learning rule is one of the most common silent failures.

Evaluation of spiking columns is under-specified in the literature. Accuracy on MNIST says little about whether you have a working column. You need sanity metrics (rates, irregularity, balance), representation metrics (sparsity, overlap, stability) and task metrics (sequence prediction, anomaly detection, sensorimotor object recognition).
Most failures are generic: runaway excitation, silent networks, dead or greedy units, time-step artefacts, unit mistakes. Knowing the symptom → cause → fix table saves a lot of time.

blocks.text: The architecture

The plan uses four functional layers. The mapping to anatomical layers follows Hawkins and colleagues and is a hypothesis about the cortex, but as an engineering design it works whether or not the brain does exactly this.

items: Input (L4-like): minicolumns of excitatory neurons. Feedforward (proximal) input is the sensed feature; context (distal) input is the current location from the location layer. Cells predicted by the location fire first and win. Output: sparse code for 'this feature at this location'.
Location (L6-like): grid-cell-like modules, each a ring (or later a 2-D sheet) of neurons holding a bump of activity. Movement shifts every bump; L4 feedback re-anchors them on a new object.

Object (L2/3-like): a pool of excitatory cells in which a stable sparse set represents the object being sensed. Fed by L4 and by long-range lateral connections from other columns' object layers, so columns vote.
Inhibition: in every layer, a pool of fast inhibitory neurons that turns dense excitation into a k-winners-take-all code with a fixed sparsity (about 2 to 5 percent active).

blocks.text: Which neuron model where

items: Excitatory cells in L4 and L2/3: LIF (#/brain/snn/neuron-models/lif) with an added dendritic compartment, or a two-compartment model (#/brain/snn/neuron-models/multicompartment). The extra compartment is what implements 'predicted': distal input depolarises the dendrite so the cell reaches threshold sooner when feedforward input arrives. A cheap alternative is a LIF neuron whose threshold drops briefly when a distal segment is active.
Inhibitory interneurons: plain LIF with short membrane time constant (about 5 to 10 ms) and fast synapses, or Izhikevich fast spiking (#/brain/snn/neuron-models/izhikevich).

Where firing patterns matter: AdEx (#/brain/snn/neuron-models/adex) or Izhikevich if you want adaptation and bursting, for instance to make bursting minicolumns literally burst. Not needed in the first version.
Avoid Hodgkin-Huxley for the column itself: it costs up to a hundred times more and adds nothing the design needs. Use it to understand spikes, not to build columns.

blocks.text: Which learning rule where

items: Feedforward into L4 (feature tuning, the spatial pooler role): competitive STDP with winner-take-all, as in Diehl and Cook (2015) and Smith's temporal neural networks. Use weight-dependent (multiplicative) STDP (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-multiplicative) so weights stay bounded, plus homeostatic threshold adaptation so all cells get used.

Distal segments in L4 (location as context): a causal, STDP-like rule that grows or strengthens synapses from cells active a moment before onto the winning cell (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-classical). In discrete form this is HTM temporal memory learning (#/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/temporal-memory).

L4 to L2/3 and L2/3 lateral (object identity and voting): Hebbian association between the stable object code and the changing L4 codes that occur while one object is sensed. A slow trace (the object code stays on across several touches) is what lets one object cell learn many feature-location codes. Triplet STDP (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-triplet) or a BCM-like rule (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-bcm) suits these rate-like associations.
Anything driven by reward or a goal later on: reward-modulated STDP with eligibility traces (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-reward).
Not needed: backpropagation or surrogate gradients (#/brain/snn/learning-rules/stdp-surrogate). They are useful baselines, but the point of a column is local, online, unsupervised learning.

blocks.text: Inhibition: the most important detail

Six LIF neurons with slightly different input strengths share an inhibitory pool. Without inhibition all six fire; with enough inhibition only the best-matched one or two do. Every stage of the column depends on this: it gives the fixed sparsity that makes codes separable, it turns 'predicted cells fire first' into 'only predicted cells fire', and it forces competing neurons to learn different features under STDP. Practical rules of thumb: make inhibition fast (time constant shorter than excitation), make it scale with total excitation rather than being a fixed amount, and measure the sparsity of every layer on every run. If learning goes wrong, check sparsity first.
Encoding the input

Encode features with population codes or latency codes (#/brain/snn/encoding) rather than raw rates: latency coding gives one spike per input per sensation, which suits the first-spike-wins logic of the input layer. For a first version, present one sensation per 'step' of 20 to 50 ms, reset fast variables between steps, and let slow ones (object layer, location bumps) persist. Synaptic filters (#/brain/snn/neuron-filters) set how long a step's spikes keep acting.
A minimum viable column (MVC) to start with

You do not need a million neurons to test column ideas. The numbers below are a deliberately small starting specification that is big enough for sparse codes to behave well (a few percent activity, low false-match probability) and small enough to simulate in seconds on a laptop in Brian2 or as a vectorised NumPy/PyTorch loop. They are a recommendation distilled from HTM defaults and the Thousand Brains papers, scaled down — not values taken from biology. Biological minicolumns contain roughly 80–120 neurons, and real columns contain thousands of minicolumns' worth of cells across six layers.

blocks.source:
MINIMUM VIABLE COLUMN (one cortical column, one sensor patch)

Encoder (input)          n = 400–1024 bits, w ≈ 2–5% active (e.g. 21 of 400)
Feature layer ("L4")     M = 256–512 minicolumns
  activity               k-WTA with k ≈ 2–4% of minicolumns (e.g. k = 10 of 256, 20 of 512)
  cells per minicolumn   8 (enough for many contexts; HTM uses 32)
  proximal inputs        each minicolumn samples ~50–80% of encoder bits (potential pool)
  distal segments        up to 16 per cell, each with up to 20–32 synapses
  segment threshold      θ ≈ 8–13 active synapses (must be < k, the number of
                         winner cells active at each step)
Inhibition               1 fast inhibitory pool, ~20–25% of the E cell count,
                         or an explicit k-WTA operator as the first version
Location layer ("L6")    4–10 grid-cell modules, each e.g. 10×10 cells, one bump
                         active per module (only needed from roadmap stage 6)
Object layer ("L2/3")    1024–4096 cells, ~40 active (stable while sensing one object)
Lateral (voting) links   object layer ↔ object layer of other columns
Time step                dt = 0.1 ms (Brian2/NEST, biophysical), 1 ms (event/vector sims)
Sensation length         one input every 10–50 ms of simulated time (one "gamma"-ish cycle)

blocks.text: Rough cell count: 256 minicolumns × 8 cells = 2,048 feature-layer cells, plus ~500 inhibitory cells and ~1,000–4,000 object-layer cells — a few thousand neurons and a few hundred thousand synapses per column. For comparison, the network in Hawkins, Ahmad & Cui (2017) used an input layer of 150 minicolumns × 16 cells and an output layer of 4,096 cells with about 40 active; Numenta's temporal memory defaults are 2,048 minicolumns × 32 cells with 40 active minicolumns (≈2%).

Two consistency rules matter more than the exact numbers. First, the distal segment threshold $\theta$ must be smaller than the number of presynaptic cells that are active at each step (with 10 active minicolumns and one winner cell each, a segment can never see more than 10 active synapses). Second, keep activity sparse but not tiny: with k below roughly 10 active units the SDR capacity and noise robustness formulas of Ahmad & Hawkins (2015, 2016) stop being reassuring.
Milestones, in order

items: 1. One neuron. Simulate LIF and a two-compartment neuron; confirm that dendritic depolarisation makes the cell fire earlier for the same input. A few hours.

2. One competitive layer. N LIF neurons with WTA inhibition and STDP on feedforward weights; train on a few fixed binary patterns (or MNIST, as in Diehl and Cook) and check that each neuron becomes selective for one pattern. Measure sparsity and selectivity.

3. Sequence memory. Add minicolumns and distal segments; train on sequences such as ABCD and XBCY and reproduce the temporal-memory result: bursting falls to near zero, and D versus Y is predicted correctly (compare the sim on #/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/temporal-memory).

4. Location layer. Build two or three ring modules with bump shifting from a movement input (ring attractor on #/brain/neuroscience/neural-manifolds); verify that combined phases code position uniquely over the range you need (grid-cell sim on #/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/reference-frames).
5. Features at locations. Replace sequence context with location context in L4. Generate synthetic objects as sets of feature-at-location pairs and train by random touches with known movements.
6. Object layer and recognition. Add the L2/3 pool with a slow trace; measure touches to recognition for a growing number of objects.

7. Many columns voting. Copy the column, give each a different sensor patch, connect object layers laterally, and reproduce the voting curve (the sim on #/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/thousand-brains).
8. Only then: realistic sensors, learned path integration, top-down feedback through apical dendrites, hierarchy.

blocks.text: Speed tip, since speed is the bottleneck: build and debug stages 2 to 7 first with binary, discrete-time HTM-style cells (minutes per experiment), then swap each layer for spiking neurons one at a time and check the measurement does not get worse. Spiking neurons add timing and energy realism, not a new algorithm, so keep the algorithm testable without them.
A minimal core loop
How the build pages fit together

A typical loop is: choose a simulator for the stage you are on (Brian2 or NEST to validate dynamics; a vectorised or PyTorch implementation to iterate quickly on learning; Lava, SpiNNaker or an FPGA once the algorithm is fixed), choose an encoder that matches what the next layer expects, add one mechanism, run the evaluation checklist, then move to the next stage of the roadmap. When something breaks, check the pitfalls page before changing three parameters at once.
Known versus speculative

items: Established: the six-layer structure and its main pathways; dendritic NMDA spikes that depolarise pyramidal cells; fast inhibition sparsifying cortical activity; STDP in many cortical synapses; grid cells and path integration in entorhinal cortex.
Well-supported models: competitive STDP layers learn features unsupervised; HTM temporal memory learns high-order sequences; continuous attractors path-integrate.

Speculative: that every column has grid-like location cells in L6; that L4 learns features at locations; that L2/3 lateral connections implement voting; that this is enough for general intelligence. Your column will be a test of these ideas, which is a good reason to build it.

blocks.text: Key takeaways

items: Build in stages and validate each stage against something you can compute or look up. Never debug the full column first.
Match encoder to learning rule: Poisson rates for STDP/Diehl & Cook-style layers, sparse overlapping SDRs for HTM-style layers.
Pick tools by stage: equation-level simulators for dynamics, vectorised/GPU code for fast iteration on learning, neuromorphic hardware only once the algorithm is stable and its constraints are known.
Report sanity metrics (rates, irregularity, balance) alongside task metrics; an MNIST number alone does not show you have a column.
Start with a minimum viable column of a few hundred minicolumns and a few thousand neurons; scale only after the stage checks pass.

blocks.text: If you only have an afternoon: build stage 1 of the roadmap (a single LIF neuron whose firing rate matches the analytic f–I curve) in the simulator you plan to use, then read the pitfalls page. Most later bugs are versions of problems you can already see at that scale.
Going deeper, in learning order

items: Simulators and Frameworks: Brian2, NEST, Nengo, Norse, snnTorch, Lava, GeNN, PyNN and BindsNET compared, with working Brian2, NEST and snnTorch code.
Neuromorphic Hardware: Loihi and Loihi 2, SpiNNaker and SpiNNaker2, TrueNorth, BrainScaleS-2 and FPGA designs, and how to map minicolumns, dendritic segments and voting onto them.
Encoding Schemes: rate (Poisson), latency, rank-order, population, delta/event-camera coding, and HTM scalar, RDSE and grid-cell encoders that produce SDRs, with code.
Evaluating a Column: sanity metrics (rates, CV of ISI, Fano factor, synchrony, E/I balance), representation metrics, task benchmarks and compute metrics, plus reproducibility.
Step-by-Step Roadmap: nine stages from tooling and a single validated LIF neuron to multiple voting columns on neuromorphic hardware, each with a goal, a validation check and pitfalls.
Common Pitfalls: a symptom → cause → fix catalogue, with an interactive raster showing what happens without inhibition.
